desc:
In the m x n matrix grid, every row and every column is sorted in non-decreasing order. Return the value stored in the grid that is closest to target (smallest absolute difference). If two different values are equally close, return the smaller one.

Try to look at only O(m + n) cells.
constraints: Each row and each column is in non-decreasing order
hints: The closest value is either the largest value ≤ target (the floor) or the smallest value ≥ target (the ceiling). Binary searching each row for both gives O(m log n).
To use the column order as well, run the usual row-and-column search for the target from the top-right corner, but do not stop when you do not find it.

Walk from the top-right: if the cell is greater than the target move left, otherwise move down. Compare every visited cell with the target and remember the best (ties go to the smaller value). The floor and the ceiling are always among the visited cells.
editorial: Whatever the target is, the answer is its floor (largest grid value ≤ target) or its ceiling (smallest grid value > target), whichever is nearer, preferring the smaller on a tie. So the task is to find the floor and the ceiling in a row- and column-sorted grid.

Run the top-right staircase walk: move left when the cell exceeds the target, move down when it does not. Claim: the walk visits a cell holding the floor and a cell holding the ceiling. For the floor, suppose its cell is (i, j) but the walk left row i by moving down from some column j' > j; then grid[i][j'] ≥ grid[i][j] and is still ≤ target, so it also holds the floor value. A symmetric argument works for the ceiling, using the left move out of column j.

So it is enough to compare every visited cell with the target and keep the best one. The walk makes at most m + n steps: O(m + n) time, O(1) space. Remember the tie rule: when two candidates are equally distant, the smaller value wins.
